l1.text: In the daytime the sky is blue, yet sunlight looks white.

l2.text: So where does the blue come from?

l3.text: In fact, white light is a mix of seven colours: red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, blue and violet.
l3.say: In fact, white light is a mix of seven colours: red, orange, yellow, green, sigh-an, blue and violet.

l4.text: Light of different colours has different wavelengths: red light has a long wavelength, blue light a short one.

l5.text: And the shorter the wavelength, the more air molecules scatter it: red light once, blue light about six times as strongly.

l6.text: As sunlight passes through the atmosphere, it keeps hitting the gas molecules in the air.

l7.text: Blue light is knocked about in every direction, while red mostly passes straight through, so wherever we look up, it is blue.

l8.text: But violet has an even shorter wavelength, so why isn't the sky violet?

l9.text: Because sunlight holds little violet to begin with, some of it is absorbed by the atmosphere, and our eyes are more sensitive to blue.

l10.text: In the evening the Sun sinks to the horizon, and its light has to cross a much thicker atmosphere.

l11.text: Along the way, nearly all the blue is scattered out, leaving only red and orange light.

l12.text: That is the colour of a sunset.
